Donatello. The early Renaissance Florentine sculptor who revolutionized the art through anatomical realism, emotional intensity, and technical innovation in marble and bronze. His figures abandon Gothic linearity for a new naturalism and psychological depth, establishing sculpture as a primary Renaissance medium.

Donatello created the first freestanding bronze David around 1440 to 1443, a youthful, unarmored figure that shocked audiences with its nudity and introspective pose. He sculpted Saint George around 1416 for Florence's Orsanmichele, a vigilant warrior-saint whose tense musculature and alert gaze defined Renaissance masculinity. Donatello pioneered bronze casting as a viable sculptural medium in the Renaissance, moving beyond the dominance of marble. He innovated linear perspective in relief sculpture, creating illusions of depth within shallow space, as seen in his Saint George and the Dragon relief.

Donatello worked for the Medici family, becoming the foundational sculptor of Florence's artistic identity. He created expressive ecclesiastical works like the marble Mary Magdalene that combined ascetic suffering with raw human pathos. His bronze David pioneered Renaissance interpretations of the biblical hero, while his Saint George launched his reputation in Florence. His innovations in realism and emotion formed the foundation upon which later Renaissance giants like Michelangelo would build.
